Then the book's loneliest verse. God describes a search He conducted Himself: “I searched for a man among them to repair the wall and stand in the gap before Me on behalf of the land, so that I should not destroy it. But I found no one.” The wall of chapter 13, the gap the false prophets refused to fill, turns out to be a vacancy God Himself advertised. One man standing in the breach, interceding, repairing, would have been enough to raise the question of mercy. In a city full of princes and priests and prophets, the search found no applicant. Ezekiel in Babylon groaned and interceded and was answered with refusal; in Jerusalem there was no one even asking. So the chapter ends with the indignation poured out and the ways of the city brought down on its own head. The indictment is complete. One chapter remains in this movement, and it is the hardest of all: the two sisters.

title: Oholah and Oholibah
subtitle: Ezekiel 23
description: Two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, carry Samaria and Jerusalem's story in the book's hardest allegory, told whole and judged in open court.
paragraphs: The movement's last allegory is its most difficult, and the book does not warn the reader or apologize for it. “Son of man, there were two women, daughters of the same mother.” They are sisters, one nation split into two kingdoms, and God gives them names that preach before the story starts: the older is Oholah, her own tent, the kingdom that set up its own shrines; the younger is Oholibah, My tent is in her, the kingdom where God's sanctuary actually stood. “As for their identities, Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem.” Both began, the allegory says, in Egypt, compromised from their youth, and both were taken into God's covenant and bore Him sons and daughters. What follows is the history of the two kingdoms told as the marital history of two sisters who could not stop running to other men, where the lovers are empires and the adultery is alliance and idolatry at once. It is told in the text's own unflinching terms, and its purpose is not titillation but nausea: the reader is meant to feel about idolatry what one feels about this.

Oholah, Samaria, goes first. While she was still God's, she lusted after the Assyrians, their governors and commanders in blue, their horsemen, the military glamour of the rising empire, and she defiled herself with Assyria's idols and never gave up the habits she had learned in Egypt. The end of her story is the pattern for her sister's: “Therefore I delivered her into the hands of her lovers, the Assyrians for whom she lusted.” The lovers turned on her. Assyria stripped her, seized her children, and put her to the sword; Samaria fell in 722 BC and the northern kingdom ceased to exist, and the allegory's cold summary is that she “became a byword among women,” a cautionary name. The whole point of telling Oholah's story first is that Oholibah watched it happen. One hundred thirty years of warning stood between Samaria's fall and Jerusalem's, written in a sister's ashes.

Oholibah's response to the warning is the allegory's central horror: “Her sister Oholibah saw this, yet in her lust and prostitution she was more depraved than her sister.” She lusted after the same Assyrians. Then she saw images of the Chaldeans engraved on a wall, officers in vermilion with flowing turbans, and lusted after pictures, and sent messengers to Babylon to invite the reality. The Babylonians came, defiled her, and she turned away from them in disgust, and then, unsatisfied still, reached back past them to Egypt, to the appetites of her youth, in verses the text renders with a bluntness that has startled readers for two thousand years and that this retelling leaves in the text's own words rather than its own. The allegory's point is the escalation itself: each lover is discarded not because she returns to her husband but because she is already looking for the next. God's summary of her is not a charge about ritual. It is personal: “Because you have forgotten Me and have cast Me behind your back, you must bear the consequences.”

So the lovers are incited against her, as Assyria was incited against Samaria, and the guest list is an army: “I will incite your lovers against you, those from whom you turned away in disgust,” the Babylonians and all the Chaldeans and the Assyrians with them, governors and commanders mounted on horses, the same desirable young men of the allegory's beginning, now arriving with weapons, chariots, buckler and shield and helmet. God delegates the judgment to them and they will carry it out by their own standards, in fury. And her punishment is figured as a drink: “Because you have followed the path of your sister, I will put her cup into your hand.” Samaria's cup, deep and wide, a cup of devastation and desolation: “You will be filled with drunkenness and grief, with a cup of devastation and desolation, the cup of your sister Samaria.” She will drink it and drain it and dash it to pieces. The sister she watched fall is not her warning anymore. She is her measure.

The chapter then starts over as a courtroom, as if the allegory needed a legal summary to sit beside it: “Son of man, will you pass judgment against Oholah and Oholibah? Then declare to them their abominations.” The charges are adultery and blood, the two words that have governed the whole movement: “For they have committed adultery, and blood is on their hands.” And the blood charge is particularized in the most damning sequence in the book: “They have even sacrificed their children, whom they bore to Me, in the fire as food for their idols,” and then, “On the very day they slaughtered their children for their idols, they entered My sanctuary to profane it.” The same day. Child sacrifice in the morning and temple worship in the afternoon, the whole horror of Judah's religion in one day's schedule. The sentence is the mob, stoning and swords, sons and daughters killed and houses burned, “So I will put an end to indecency in the land.” And the refrain lands on the sisters as it has landed on every subject of this movement: “Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.”

title: The Pot and the Desire of Your Eyes
subtitle: Ezekiel 24
description: On the day the siege begins, a cooking pot preaches Jerusalem's end, and the desire of Ezekiel's eyes is taken in a single evening.
paragraphs: The last chapter of the judgment movement opens with the most precisely dated sentence in the book, and God orders it written down like a legal record. “In the ninth year, on the tenth day of the tenth month, the word of the LORD came to me, saying, ‘Son of man, write down today’s date, for on this very day the king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem.” Five hundred miles away, on the day the siege ramps go up around Jerusalem, a prophet in Babylon is told to date his diary. Years later, when the fugitive arrives with the news, the exiles will be able to check the date against the siege's beginning and know that their prophet had been told in real time. The sign that follows is the pot of chapter 11 come back, but the leaders' snug proverb is now a parable of doom: put the pot on, fill it with the choicest pieces and bones, pile the fuel, bring it to a boil.

God's interpretation turns the cooking into an autopsy. “Woe to the city of bloodshed, to the pot now rusted, whose rust will not come off! Empty it piece by piece; cast no lots for its contents.” No lots: no choosing who goes out, no favoritism in the emptying, every piece removed. The rust is the city's corruption, and its evidence is the blood: “For the blood she shed is still within her; she poured it out on the bare rock; she did not pour it on the ground to cover it with dust.” Blood shed in the open, uncovered, unashamed, left on the rock where God deliberately kept it visible “so that it would not be covered,” a standing exhibit. So the fire is piled high, the meat cooked well, the bones burned, and then the empty pot itself is set on the coals until its copper glows, to burn the rust out of the metal. And the rust stays. “It has frustrated every effort; its thick rust has not been removed, even by the fire.” God states His own history with the city as a failed cleansing: “I tried to cleanse you, but you would not be purified from your filthiness. You will not be pure again until My wrath against you has subsided.” Then the seal: “I, the LORD, have spoken; the time is coming, and I will act. I will not refrain or show pity, nor will I relent.”

Then the word comes a second time that day, and it is not about Jerusalem. “Son of man, behold, I am about to take away the desire of your eyes with a fatal blow. But you must not mourn or weep or let your tears flow.” The desire of Ezekiel's eyes is his wife. The text gives her no name, no words, no scene of her own, only that title, and it is enough: she is what he loves to look at, and she will die suddenly, today, and her husband the prophet is forbidden the entire human apparatus of grief. “Groan quietly; do not mourn for the dead. Put on your turban and strap your sandals on your feet; do not cover your lips or eat the bread of mourners.” No sackcloth, no bare head, no covered face, no sympathy meals from the neighbors, none of the customs by which his culture carried the bereaved. He is to dress for an ordinary day. And the record of his obedience is the flattest sentence in the book, three clauses with no comment: “So I spoke to the people in the morning, and in the evening my wife died. And the next morning I did as I had been commanded.”

The sign works the way signs work on this audience: they finally ask a question. “Won’t you tell us what these things you are doing mean to us?” And the explanation reveals why the prophet's marriage had to become his last sermon illustration. Jerusalem has a desire of its eyes too: “I am about to desecrate My sanctuary, the pride of your power, the desire of your eyes, and the delight of your soul. And the sons and daughters you left behind will fall by the sword.” The temple and the children, taken in one blow, the sanctuary by desecration and the sons and daughters by the sword. And when it happens, the people will discover in themselves the same unnatural paralysis Ezekiel modeled: “You will not mourn or weep, but you will waste away because of your sins, and you will groan among yourselves.” Grief too large for its rituals, a nation doing as he did because it can do nothing else. “Thus Ezekiel will be a sign for you; you will do everything that he has done. When this happens, you will know that I am the Lord GOD.”

The chapter, and with it the whole judgment movement, ends on a promise made to the silenced prophet personally, a date set in the future that he cannot yet see. “on the day I take away their stronghold,” God says, “on that day a fugitive will come and tell you the news. On that day your mouth will be opened to him who has escaped; you will speak and no longer be mute. So you will be a sign to them, and they will know that I am the LORD.” The siege has begun. The fugitive is two and a half years away, running through a war. Between this chapter and that arrival stretches the long silence of the prophet and, in the book's arrangement, the oracles against the nations, the words God speaks to everyone else while Jerusalem burns down to its conclusion. The movement that began with glory arriving in Babylon ends with a wife's death in Babylon and a city's death begun in Jerusalem, and the prophet who has performed his own bereavement sits down to wait for the runner.

title: Aha!
subtitle: Ezekiel 25
description: The word turns outward: Ammon's cheer, Moab's sneer, Edom's vengeance, and the Philistines' ancient grudge each receive their sentence.
paragraphs: The nations section opens with the near neighbors, and it opens with a sound. Ammon, Judah's relative across the Jordan, watched the sanctuary burn and the king go into exile and said one word about it. God quotes the word: “Aha!” The oracle spells out what the one syllable celebrated: “when My sanctuary was profaned, when the land of Israel was laid waste, and when the house of Judah went into exile.” Ammon's whole indictment is a cheer at a funeral. The second charge adds the hands and feet: “Because you clapped your hands and stomped your feet and rejoiced over the land of Israel with a heart full of contempt.” Gloating is the sin, contempt the fuel, and the sentence fits the geography: Ammon will be given to the people of the East, desert tribes who will camp in its cities and eat its fruit, until its capital becomes what it mocked others for becoming: “I will make Rabbah a pasture for camels, and Ammon a resting place for sheep. Then you will know that I am the LORD.”

Moab's sin is a sentence instead of a cheer, and the sentence is a sneer: “Look, the house of Judah is like all the other nations.” Moab, Judah's other ancient relative, looked at the covenant people in their ruin and concluded that their God had been a fiction, that Judah was ordinary all along and its claims a pretense. The judgment answers the sneer by erasing the border Moab was proud of: God will expose Moab's flank, beginning with its frontier cities, “the glory of the land,” and hand the whole to the people of the East together with Ammon, “so that the Ammonites will no longer be remembered among the nations.” To be forgotten among the nations is the sentence, an un-nationing, and Moab shares it for deciding that God's people were nothing special. “So I will execute judgments on Moab, and they will know that I am the LORD.”

Edom's oracle is the one this series has heard building for three books. “Because Edom acted vengefully against the house of Judah, and in so doing incurred grievous guilt,” God will stretch out His hand against Edom and make it a wasteland, from Teman to Dedan its people falling by the sword. Obadiah's whole book argued this case: the brother who stood aloof on the day of disaster, who gloated, looted, cut down fugitives, and handed over survivors. Jeremiah's prophets spoke against Edom too.

Here the sentence names the executioner, and it is the twist no one in Edom would expect: “I will take My vengeance on Edom by the hand of My people Israel, and they will deal with Edom according to My anger and wrath. Then they will know My vengeance, declares the Lord GOD.” The exiled, scattered, temple-less people will one day be the hand of God's vengeance on the brother who kicked them as they fell. Edom's judgment is deferred into Israel's restoration, which means this short oracle contains a future neither nation could see from the ruins.

The Philistines, the old coastal enemy from the days of the judges and David, are charged with the mirror image of Edom's sin: “Because the Philistines acted in vengeance, taking vengeance with malice of soul to destroy Judah with ancient hostility.” Ancient hostility, vengeance nursed for centuries and fed at Judah's collapse. God will cut off the Cherethites and destroy the remnant along the coast: “I will execute great vengeance against them with furious reproof. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I lay My vengeance upon them.” Four oracles, four refrains of recognition. The pattern of the section is now set: the nations are not judged for failing to be Israel. They are judged for what they did with Israel's fall, the cheer, the sneer, the vengeance, the malice, and behind the judgments stands the claim that has run through the whole book: the God of Israel is the LORD of the nations too, and He keeps accounts on both sides of Judah's borders.

title: The Bare Rock
subtitle: Ezekiel 26
description: Tyre laughed at Jerusalem's fall and gets three chapters: her walls unbuilt stone by stone until she is a bare rock for spreading nets.
paragraphs: Tyre gets three chapters where Ammon got half of one, because Tyre's sin is bigger and so is Tyre. The oracle is dated to the twelfth year of the exile, after Jerusalem's fall, and it begins by quoting Tyre's boardroom assessment of the catastrophe. Tyre was the Mediterranean's great trading power, an island fortress-city off the Phoenician coast, and Jerusalem had been its inland competitor on the trade routes. Tyre's verdict on the news: “Aha! The gate to the nations is broken; it has swung open to me; now that she lies in ruins I will be filled.” The gate is broken, the traffic reroutes through us, her ruin is our revenue. It is Ammon's “Aha!” with an accounting department. God's answer begins with the book's most personal formula: “Behold, O Tyre, I am against you, and I will raise up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves.” Wave after wave of nations, against the city that ruled the waves.

What the waves will do is described as an un-building. “They will destroy the walls of Tyre and demolish her towers. I will scrape the soil from her and make her a bare rock.” Scrape the soil: the island will be reduced to its geology. “She will become a place to spread nets in the sea, for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD. She will become plunder for the nations.” Fishermen drying nets where the counting houses stood. The mainland villages, Tyre's suburbs and supply towns, will fall by the sword first. And then God does something unusual in these oracles: He names the wave. “Behold, I will bring against Tyre from the north Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings, with horses and chariots, with cavalry and a great company of troops.” Nebuchadnezzar, fresh from Jerusalem, is God's named instrument against Tyre, as he was against Judah, and the siege is narrated in advance in his own tactics: siege works, a ramp built to the walls, shields raised, battering rams directed blow by blow.

The city's fall is told in sensory detail. His horses will be so many that “their dust” covers the city; the walls will shake “from the noise of cavalry, wagons, and chariots” as he enters “as an army entering a breached city.” Hooves trample every street; the people fall by the sword; the “mighty pillars” of her temples and palaces fall to the ground.

Then the plunder is not merely taken, it is disposed of in a way that preaches: “They will plunder your wealth and pillage your merchandise. They will demolish your walls, tear down your beautiful homes, and throw your stones and timber and soil into the water.” Tyre's substance goes into the sea that made her rich, rubble into the harbor, which is how an island city gets scraped to rock: her own ruins become the fill. And with the wealth goes the music: “So I will silence the sound of your songs, and the music of your lyres will no longer be heard.” The oracle's verdict on permanence is absolute: “I will make you a bare rock, and you will become a place to spread the fishing nets. You will never be rebuilt, for I, the LORD, have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.”

The reaction shots belong to Tyre's trading partners, the princes of the sea, the merchant kings of the coastlands. At the sound of her fall they come down off their thrones, strip off their robes and embroidered garments, clothe themselves with terror, and sit on the ground “trembling every moment, appalled over you.” Their lament is quoted, and it is genuinely astonished: “How you have perished, O city of renown inhabited by seafaring men,” “she who was powerful on the sea, along with her people, who imposed terror on all peoples!” The woman who imposed terror is now the object of it, and the islands tremble at her demise. The oracle's last movement takes her below the world entirely: God will raise the deep over her, bring her down “with those who descend to the Pit, to the people of antiquity,” to dwell in the earth below among ancient ruins, uninhabited forever. “I will make you an object of horror, and you will be no more. You will be sought, but will never be found,’ declares the Lord GOD.” Sought, and never found. The next chapter sings her funeral as a shipwreck.

title: The Ship of Tyre
subtitle: Ezekiel 27
description: A funeral song for a living city reads Tyre's cargo manifest like a list of the dead, then an east wind breaks the great ship on the high seas.
paragraphs: God orders a funeral song for a city that has not fallen yet: “Now you, son of man, take up a lament for Tyre.” And the lament's controlling image is not a rock this time but a ship, the most beautiful ship in the world, built in the poem plank by plank out of the whole Mediterranean's best materials. Tyre is addressed first by her own slogan: “You have said, O Tyre, ‘I am perfect in beauty.’” The poem grants the claim before it sinks it. “Your borders are in the heart of the seas; your builders perfected your beauty.” Her planking is cypress from Senir. “They took a cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you.” Her oars are Bashan oak, her deck wood from Cyprus inlaid with ivory, and “Of embroidered fine linen from Egypt they made your sail, which served as your banner,” with awnings of blue and purple from the coasts of Elishah. A merchant ship built like a royal yacht, every material imported, every detail finished.

The crew and the guard are as international as the cargo. The men of Sidon and Arvad, Phoenicia's other ports, are her oarsmen; Tyre's own skilled men are her captains; the elders of Gebal are aboard as shipwrights, caulking her leaks while she sails. Her army is hired from three continents: “Men of Persia, Lydia, and Put served as warriors in your army. They hung their shields and helmets on your walls; they gave you splendor.” Arvad and Helech man the walls, the Gammadim hold the towers, shields hung all around, until the poem repeats Tyre's slogan as a shipyard verdict: they “perfected your beauty.” A city whose defense, labor, and luxury were all somebody else's work, assembled and financed by Tyre, floating on the sea she believed she owned.

Then the manifest, and the poem slows down to read the cargo list the way a mourner reads names. Tarshish, at the far western end of the world, trades silver, iron, tin, and lead. Javan, Tubal, and Meshech trade in slaves and bronze. Beth-togarmah sends horses and mules; Dedan pays in ivory tusks and ebony; Aram in turquoise, coral, and rubies. And in the middle of the list, quietly, stands Judah: “Judah and the land of Israel traded with you; they exchanged wheat from Minnith, cakes and honey, oil and balm for your merchandise.” God's own people were among her suppliers, which is part of the lament's tragedy; the trade web held everyone. Damascus sends wine and wool, Arabia lambs and rams and goats, Sheba and Raamah “gold, the finest of all spices, and precious stones,” and the ships of Tarshish haul it all, until the summary lands: “The ships of Tarshish carried your merchandise. And you were filled with heavy cargo in the heart of the sea.” Filled, and heavy. The poem has been loading the ship for twenty verses so the reader will feel the weight of what goes down.

The wreck takes three verses. “Your oarsmen have brought you onto the high seas, but the east wind will shatter you in the heart of the sea.” The east wind, for the third time in this book, is the wind God sends, Babylon's wind, and against it the perfect beauty has no defense at all. “Your wealth, wares, and merchandise, your sailors, captains, and shipwrights, your merchants and all the warriors within you, with all the other people on board, will sink into the heart of the sea on the day of your downfall.” Everything itemized in the manifest sinks in one catalogue reversed: wealth, crew, guard, passengers, all of it, in the depths of the waters.

The final scene is the shore. The sailors and captains who escape abandon their ships and stand on the beach and perform the mourning of the ancient world at full volume: dust on their heads, rolling in ashes, heads shaved, sackcloth, weeping “with anguish of soul and bitter mourning.” Their lament over her is the chapter's epitaph: “Who was ever like Tyre, silenced in the middle of the sea?” The kings of the coastlands shudder, their faces contorted; the traders among the nations hiss. And the poem ends with the sentence that has followed Tyre through all three chapters, now pronounced over her wreck: “you have come to a horrible end and will be no more.” One more Tyre oracle remains, the most personal of all, addressed not to the city but to its king, and it reaches back further than trade, to Eden.

title: I Am a God; the Guardian Cherub
subtitle: Ezekiel 28
description: A prince who called himself a god, a king pictured in Eden beside a guardian cherub, and a short, settled word for Israel close the Tyre oracles.
paragraphs: The last Tyre oracles are addressed to two figures, the ruler and the king, and the first is charged with the sentence Tyre's wealth finally produced. “Your heart is proud, and you have said, ‘I am a god; I sit in the seat of gods in the heart of the sea.’” An island throne, a harbor full of gold, a city no army had ever taken, and the man on top of it concludes he is divine. God's answer is the shortest theology of man in the book: “Yet you are a man and not a god, though you have regarded your heart as that of a god.” The sarcasm that follows uses Ezekiel's own contemporary: “Behold, you are wiser than Daniel; no secret is hidden from you!” Daniel, the exile in Babylon's court, famous in this book already as a standard of righteousness, is here the standard of wisdom, and Tyre's king is conceded the title in mockery, because his wisdom was real and it was all spent on one thing: “By your wisdom and understanding you have gained your wealth and amassed gold and silver for your treasuries.” Wisdom as a money machine, and the machine's exhaust is pride.

The sentence imports the executioners: foreigners, “the most ruthless of nations,” will draw swords against the beauty of his wisdom and bring him down to the Pit to “die a violent death in the heart of the seas.” And the oracle ends with a question to be answered at swordpoint: “Will you still say, ‘I am a god,’ in the presence of those who slay you? You will be only a man, not a god, in the hands of those who wound you.” Divinity claims do not survive contact with the men sent to test them. The ruler of Tyre will die the death of the uncircumcised at foreign hands, a nobody's death, and the distance between the seat of gods and that ditch is exactly the distance the oracle intends to measure.

Then the lament for the king, and the language changes register entirely. “You were the seal of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. You were in Eden, the garden of God.” The poem clothes him in the high priest's own stones, ruby, topaz, diamond, beryl, onyx, jasper, sapphire, turquoise, emerald, set in gold “prepared on the day of your creation,” and stations him where no merchant ever stood: “You were anointed as a guardian cherub, for I had ordained you. You were on the holy mountain of God; you walked among the fiery stones.” And the fall, when it comes, is dated with terrible simplicity: “From the day you were created you were blameless in your ways,” and then, as a separate fragment of the same sentence, “until wickedness was found in you.” The wickedness is specified, and it is Tyre's own: by the vastness of his trade he was filled with violence and sinned; his heart grew proud of his beauty; he corrupted his wisdom for the sake of his splendor. So the guardian is banished from the mountain and the fiery stones, cast to the earth, made a spectacle before kings, and burned from within: fire comes out of him and reduces him to ashes on the ground in the eyes of all who saw him. The lament is addressed to the king of Tyre, and it is told here as addressed to him; its Eden and cherub language has carried readers further, into readings about the fall of Satan, and that identification belongs to interpretation, held by many and argued by others, while the text's own address stands on the king whose pride it buries.

Sidon, Tyre's sister city up the coast, gets a short oracle of her own: plague, blood in her streets, the sword on every side, and the purpose stated in the refrain, that she will know that He is the LORD. With her judgment comes a small mercy for Israel tucked inside it: “For the people of Israel will no longer face a pricking brier or a painful thorn from all around them who treat them with contempt.” The contemptuous neighbors, named through this whole section, are being cleared away one by one, and not for their own sake.

That clearing makes room for the section's last word, and it is not addressed to any nation. It is the first gathering promise since chapter 11, and it lands in the middle of the nations oracles like light through a wall: “When I gather the house of Israel from the peoples among whom they have been scattered, I will show Myself holy among them in the sight of the nations. Then they will dwell in their own land, which I have given to My servant Jacob. And there they will dwell securely, build houses, and plant vineyards.” Build houses and plant vineyards: the ordinary life whose loss Jeremiah's exiles mourned, promised back as the content of restoration. The nations' section is not finished; Egypt, the biggest name of all, still waits. But its direction is now visible. The judgments on the nations are not a detour from Israel's story. They are the ground being cleared around a people God intends to bring home, and the last line of the Tyre cycle is the refrain turned possessive at last: “Then they will know that I am the LORD their God.”

title: The Monster in the Nile
subtitle: Ezekiel 29
description: Egypt is a monster in his own river, hooked and hauled out, and the latest-dated oracle in the book pays Babylon's wages in Egyptian land.
paragraphs: Egypt is the last and largest of the nations, and it gets the longest treatment, four chapters answering to Tyre's three, because Egypt is not merely a proud trading power. Egypt is Israel's oldest temptation, the ally every generation reached for, and its king is addressed as something older and stranger than a man. The oracle is dated in the tenth year, while Jerusalem still stood under siege: “set your face against Pharaoh king of Egypt and prophesy against him and against all Egypt.” The charge is a sentence Pharaoh says about the river that made his country: “Behold, I am against you, O Pharaoh king of Egypt, O great monster who lies among his rivers, who says, ‘The Nile is mine; I made it myself.’” The Nile is not a river in Egypt's theology; it is life itself, rising every year without rain, and Pharaoh claims authorship of it. I made it myself. It is the Tyre king's “I am a god” in hydraulic form.

God's answer treats the monster as a fish too big for his own river. “But I will put hooks in your jaws and cause the fish of your streams to cling to your scales. I will haul you up out of your rivers,” and the whole catch, monster and fish together, will be left “in the desert,” to “fall on the open field and will not be taken away or gathered for burial,” given as food to beasts and birds. A water god dying unburied on dry land: the image is the whole judgment in one picture. And Egypt's specific crime against Israel is named in a metaphor any Israelite who had leaned on Egypt could feel in his shoulder: “For you were only a staff of reeds to the house of Israel. When Israel took hold of you with their hands, you splintered, tearing all their shoulders; when they leaned on you, you broke, and their backs were wrenched.” A reed staff looks like support and behaves like a blade. Zedekiah's embassy, Judah's whole Egyptian policy across centuries, is summed up in a splintered reed tearing the hand that trusted it.

The sentence is desolation with a map attached: Egypt will become “a ruin, a desolate wasteland from Migdol to Syene, and as far as the border of Cush,” north to south, the whole river kingdom. “No foot of man or beast will pass through, and it will be uninhabited for forty years,” its cities desolate among desolate lands, its people dispersed among the nations like Israel's own. And then, uniquely among the nations in this section, Egypt is given an after: “At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the nations to which they were scattered” and restore them to Pathros, their ancient homeland in the south, where “There they will be a lowly kingdom. Egypt will be the lowliest of kingdoms and will never again exalt itself above the nations.” Egypt survives, diminished on purpose, and its survival has a function in Israel's education: “Egypt will never again be an object of trust for the house of Israel, but will remind them of their iniquity in turning to the Egyptians.” The reed will still be there, too weak to lean on, a permanent museum of Israel's folly.

The chapter's second oracle is dated later than any other in the book, the twenty-seventh year, and it explains Egypt's fall as a payroll transaction. Nebuchadnezzar's thirteen-year siege of Tyre had ended with little plunder; the island's wealth escaped by sea, and his army's labor went unpaid: “Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon caused his army to labor strenuously against Tyre. Every head was made bald and every shoulder made raw. But he and his army received no wages from Tyre for the labor they expended on it.” So God pays His workman: “I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who will carry off its wealth, seize its spoil, and remove its plunder. This will be the wages for his army.” And the ground of the payment is the book's boldest statement about empire: “I have given him the land of Egypt as the reward for his labor, because it was done for Me, declares the Lord GOD.” Babylon's wars, in this accounting, were God's projects, and Egypt is the paycheck.

The oracle ends with two promises tied to the same day. “In that day I will cause a horn to sprout for the house of Israel,” a horn being strength, a king's rising power, sprouting while Egypt is plundered, “and I will open your mouth to speak among them. Then they will know that I am the LORD.” The sprouting horn echoes the tender sprig of chapter 17, God's own planting. The opened mouth is the second time the book has promised it; the first was the night Ezekiel's wife died, tied to a fugitive's arrival. The two promises now stand side by side at the end of the Egypt cycle, waiting for the same runner.

title: The Day of Clouds
subtitle: Ezekiel 30
description: A day of clouds for Egypt: fire, shattered allies, a roll of famous cities, and Pharaoh's arm broken a second time, beyond setting.
paragraphs: Chapter 30 opens with a command to wail and a name for what is coming that this book has used for Judah and now uses for the world: “For the day is near, the Day of the LORD is near. It will be a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations.” Clouds, not light: the Day of the LORD arrives over Egypt as weather. A sword comes against Egypt, anguish seizes Cush to the south, Egypt's wealth is carried off and her foundations torn down, and the casualty list is her alliance system: “Cush, Put, and Lud, and all the various peoples, as well as Libya and the men of the covenant land, will fall with Egypt by the sword.” Egypt never fought alone; her mercenaries and client peoples fall with her, and the summary is geographical and total: “The allies of Egypt will fall, and her proud strength will collapse. From Migdol to Syene they will fall by the sword within her, declares the Lord GOD.”

God will set fire to Egypt and shatter all her helpers, and the news will travel faster than the army: messengers go out in ships “to frighten Cush out of complacency,” doom announced down the Nile before it arrives, so that even the warning is part of the terror. The instrument is named again, as it was for Tyre: “I will put an end to the hordes of Egypt by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. He and his people with him, the most ruthless of the nations, will be brought in to destroy the land.” The rivers, Egypt's life, are given away in one commercial phrase: “I will make the streams dry up and sell the land to the wicked.” And the judgment reaches the gods: “I will destroy the idols and put an end to the images in Memphis. There will no longer be a prince in Egypt, and I will instill fear in that land.” Memphis, the ancient capital, loses its images; Egypt loses its prince; a kingdom older than Israel by a millennium is told its monarchy and its pantheon end together.

Then the oracle walks the map city by city, a drumbeat of famous names receiving sentences. Pathros in the south will be laid waste, Zoan set on fire, judgment executed on Thebes, the great southern capital with its temples. Wrath is poured on Pelusium, Egypt's eastern stronghold, the fortress on the invasion road. Thebes will be split open, Memphis in daily distress, the young men of On and Pi-beseth fallen by the sword and their cities in captivity. “The day will be darkened in Tahpanhes when I break the yoke of Egypt and her proud strength comes to an end. A cloud will cover her, and her daughters will go into captivity.” The cloud of the chapter's opening settles, by its end, on one named town after another. The whole oracle reads like a siege itinerary written by the besieger's employer.

The chapter's second half is dated in the eleventh year and brings the metaphor down to one body, Pharaoh's. “I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt. See, it has not been bound up for healing, or splinted for strength to hold the sword.” The arm is broken already, historically by Babylon's earlier victory, and heaven's point is that no physician has been allowed near it: the break is permanent by decree. “Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt. I will break his arms, both the strong one and the one already broken, and will make the sword fall from his hand.” And the counterpart is stated in the same breath, the two kings' arms treated as God's own equipment decisions: “I will strengthen the arms of Babylon’s king and place My sword in his hand, but I will break the arms of Pharaoh, who will groan before him like a mortally wounded man.” My sword in his hand. Nebuchadnezzar does not know he is armed by God; the exiles reading Ezekiel do.

The chapter closes with the dispersion formula applied to Egypt as it was applied to Israel, twice in three verses, as if to make the symmetry impossible to miss: “I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands. Then they will know that I am the LORD.” Scattering was Israel's covenant curse; here it is Egypt's portion too, and the recognition refrain, they will know that I am the LORD, is promised to Egyptians as it was to Israelites. The nations section has been building this equation since Ammon: one God, one standard, every nation on the same ledger. One Egypt oracle remains, and it is a funeral: first a tree, then a graveyard.

title: The Cedar in Eden and the Tour of the Pit
subtitle: Ezekiel 31-32
description: A cedar that towered over Eden explains Egypt's fall, and the last lament walks Pharaoh down into the Pit to lie among the empires already there.
paragraphs: To explain Egypt, Ezekiel is told to tell Pharaoh about a tree that is already dead. “Look at Assyria, a cedar in Lebanon, with beautiful branches that shaded the forest. It towered on high; its top was among the clouds.” Assyria, the empire that destroyed Samaria and terrified the world, is remembered in its glory deliberately and at length: the deep springs watered it until it towered over every tree in the field, its branches multiplied, and the whole world lived off it: “All the birds of the air nested in its branches, and all the beasts of the field gave birth beneath its boughs; all the great nations lived in its shade.” Its beauty is conceded in the strongest available comparison: “The cedars in the garden of God could not rival it,” and God claims the artistry personally: “I made it beautiful with its many branches, the envy of all the trees of Eden, which were in the garden of God.” Egypt is being measured against the greatest empire the region had known, and the measurement is not an insult. It is a setup.

The fall of the cedar is told as the pattern of all imperial falls. “Since it became great in height and set its top among the clouds, and it grew proud on account of its height, I delivered it into the hand of the ruler of the nations, for him to deal with it according to its wickedness.” Pride in height is the charge; height itself was God's gift. “Foreigners, the most ruthless of the nations, cut it down and left it,” branches fallen on the mountains, boughs broken in every ravine, and “all the peoples of the earth left its shade and abandoned it.” The nations that nested in it now nest on its corpse. And the felling has a stated purpose for every tree still standing: “This happened so that no other trees by the waters would become great in height and set their tops among the clouds.” The cedar is a sermon other empires were meant to hear. Egypt is hearing it in this chapter, which means Egypt, like Judah before her, is being given the warning in time and will be judged for ignoring it exactly as Assyria was the warning to her.

When the cedar went down, the underworld itself reacted: God caused mourning, restrained the waters, made Lebanon faint, and “I made the nations quake at the sound of its downfall, when I cast it down to Sheol with those who descend to the Pit. Then all the trees of Eden, the choicest and best of Lebanon, all the well-watered trees, were consoled in the earth below.” Consoled: the dead empires in the Pit took comfort that the greatest had joined them. Then the application turns and points at the living king: “Who then is like you in glory and greatness among the trees of Eden? You also will be brought down to the depths of the earth to be with the trees of Eden. You will lie among the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword. This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD.” Your glory is like Assyria's. Your end will be Assyria's. The tree sermon is over, and chapter 32 sings the funeral.

The last Egypt oracle is a lament dated in the twelfth year, and it opens by merging Pharaoh's two animals: “You are like a lion among the nations; you are like a monster in the seas. You thrash about in your rivers, churning up the waters with your feet and muddying the streams.” Lion on land, monster in the water, and the net spread for him by a company of peoples will haul him out to die on dry ground under an extinguished sky: “When I extinguish you, I will cover the heavens and darken their stars. I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon will not give its light.” Kings in countries he does not know will tremble for their own lives at the news. “The sword of the king of Babylon will come against you,” the ruthless of all nations will ravage Egypt's pride, her cattle will be slaughtered beside waters no foot will muddy again, until the rivers of Egypt run clear and still: “Then I will let her waters settle and will make her rivers flow like oil.” The lament will become a standard song: “This is the lament they will chant for her; the daughters of the nations will chant it. Over Egypt and all her multitudes they will chant it, declares the Lord GOD.”

Then the prophet is told to wail Egypt down into the Pit personally and take the tour. “Whom do you surpass in beauty? Go down and be placed with the uncircumcised!” In Sheol the mighty chiefs speak, and their one line welcomes every arrival: “They have come down and lie with the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword.” Grave by grave the roll is called. “Assyria is there with her whole company; her graves are all around her. All of them are slain, fallen by the sword,” those who once spread terror in the land of the living. Elam is there, bearing her disgrace. Meshech and Tubal are there, uncircumcised, their terror spent. Edom is there, with all her kings and princes, laid among the slain despite their might. The leaders of the north and the Sidonians are there, gone down in disgrace. One refrain walks the whole cemetery: they spread terror in the land of the living, and they lie here. And the tour's last sight is the comfort Pharaoh is offered, the only comfort the Pit has: “Pharaoh will see them and be comforted over all his multitude.” Comforted, by the company. The nations section ends in that graveyard, with Egypt laid among her predecessors, and the book turns, at last, back to the prophet in Babylon, where a runner is already on the road.

title: The City Has Fallen
subtitle: Ezekiel 33
description: The watchman charter is preached again to a changed audience, a runner arrives from Jerusalem, and Ezekiel's mouth is opened at last.
paragraphs: The book's second half begins by repeating its commission, and the repetition is the signal that everything has changed. God gives Ezekiel the watchman doctrine again, nearly word for word from chapter 3: the land appoints a watchman, the watchman blows the ram's horn, whoever hears and ignores it has his blood on his own head, and the watchman who fails to blow it answers for the blood himself. “As for you, O son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; so hear the word from My mouth and give them the warning from Me.” In chapter 3 this was the charter of a ministry of warning before the fall. Here it is reissued after the fall has already been decreed, to a prophet whose judgment oracles are finished, and the doctrine's emphasis shifts underneath the same words: the point is no longer only accountability. The wicked who turns will live. The charter of the book's second half is a charter of rescue.

The audience has changed first. The exiles who once quoted proverbs about delay now say something new, and God quotes their despair back to them: “Our transgressions and our sins are heavy upon us, and we are wasting away because of them! How can we live?” It is the first honest sentence the exiles speak in the book, and it gets the book's most impassioned answer, sworn on God's own life: “As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked should turn from their ways and live. Turn! Turn from your evil ways! For why should you die, O house of Israel?” Turn, twice, like a man shouting. Chapter 18's doctrine is preached again with the volume raised: the righteous man's righteousness “will not deliver him in the day of his transgression,” and the wicked man who turns, who restores a pledge and “makes restitution for what he has stolen,” finds that “None of the sins he has committed will be held against him. He has done what is just and right; he will surely live.” The people grumble one more time that the way of the Lord is not just, and are answered the same way: it is their way that is not just, and God will judge each according to his ways.

Then the runner arrives. “In the twelfth year of our exile, on the fifth day of the tenth month, a fugitive from Jerusalem came to me and reported, ‘The city has been taken!’” Five words, and the siege that began the day Ezekiel's wife died has ended the way every oracle said it would. And the detail the prophet records is the timing of his own release: “Now the evening before the fugitive arrived, the hand of the LORD was upon me, and He opened my mouth before the man came to me in the morning. So my mouth was opened and I was no longer mute.” God opened his mouth the night before the news got there, fulfilling to the hour the promise made in chapter 24 on the day of the bereavement, and echoed in the Egypt oracle: in that day I will open your mouth. The silenced prophet speaks again, permanently, and the first subject of his restored voice is not Jerusalem's corpse but her future.

Not everyone hears the news the same way. In the ruins back home, the survivors are making a land claim: “Abraham was only one man, yet he possessed the land. But we are many; surely the land has been given to us as a possession.” Numbers as title deed, Abraham as precedent. God's answer strips the arithmetic: “You eat meat with the blood in it, lift up your eyes to your idols, and shed blood. Should you then possess the land?” Twice the question is asked, and the verdict is sword, wild animals, and plague for the remnant in the ruins, and a land made desolate waste until no one passes through. Possession, in this book, was never a head count. It was always a holiness question, and the ruins' inhabitants have answered it wrong with blood in their food and idols in their eyes.

The chapter closes with the audience Ezekiel actually has, and it is the most quietly devastating portrait in the book. The exiles talk about him at the walls and in their doorways, inviting each other like concertgoers: come and hear the message that has come from the LORD. They come, they sit, they hear, “but they do not put them into practice. Although they express love with their mouths, their hearts pursue dishonest gain. Indeed, you are to them like a singer of love songs with a beautiful voice, who skillfully plays an instrument. They hear your words but do not put them into practice.” The prophet as entertainment, judgment as a love song, a voice admired and a message shelved. God's comment on the whole arrangement returns to the criterion of the original commission, now nearly six years old: “So when it comes to pass,” and surely it will come, “then they will know that a prophet has been among them.” It has come to pass. The nursing of the exiles' hearts, song by song, sermon by sermon, is the work of the book's remaining fifteen chapters.

title: Woe to the Shepherds
subtitle: Ezekiel 34
description: God audits the shepherds who fed themselves, dismisses them, and promises the flock one shepherd, His servant David, and a covenant of peace.
paragraphs: With the kings gone, God audits the institution that produced them. “Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel. Prophesy and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” Shepherd is the Bible's standing title for rulers, and the indictment is a job description read backwards. “You eat the fat, wear the wool, and butcher the fattened sheep, but you do not feed the flock.” The produce of the flock flows one direction, into the shepherds. Then the neglected duties are listed, five of them, each one a sheep in trouble: “You have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bound up the injured, brought back the strays, or searched for the lost. Instead, you have ruled them with violence and cruelty.” Strengthen, heal, bind up, bring back, search: that is the whole office, and Israel's shepherds replaced all five verbs with two, violence and cruelty.

The flock's condition follows from the shepherds' as effect from cause. “They were scattered for lack of a shepherd, and when they were scattered they became food for all the wild beasts.” God's own summary dwells on the loneliness of it: “My flock went astray on all the mountains and every high hill. They were scattered over the face of all the earth, with no one to search for them or seek them out.” No one searched. The exile, in this chapter's analysis, is not first a military fact but a pastoral one: sheep scattered because shepherds fed themselves. So God dissolves the institution: “Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will demand from them My flock and remove them from tending the flock, so that they can no longer feed themselves. For I will deliver My flock from their mouths, and it will no longer be food for them.” My flock, demanded back out of their mouths. The possessive does the sentencing.

Then comes the sentence the whole chapter exists to reach, spoken with the book's signature emphasis: “Behold, I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out.” I Myself. God takes the shepherd's crook personally, and the five neglected verbs come back as His own program, expanded: “As a shepherd looks for his scattered sheep when he is among the flock, so I will look for My flock. I will rescue them from all the places to which they were scattered on a day of clouds and darkness.” He will bring them out from the peoples, gather them from the countries, feed them on the mountains of Israel in good pasture, and make them lie down. “I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak; but the sleek and strong I will destroy. I will shepherd them with justice.” Every verb the shepherds skipped, God performs, and the justice clause cuts both ways: the weak get binding up, and the strong who got fat on the flock get destroyed.

For the flock itself also needs judging, and the chapter's middle section is God refereeing sheep. Some sheep are fat and violent: they eat the good pasture and trample the rest, drink the clear water and muddy what is left, and the prophet gives their question its full sarcasm: “Is it not enough for you to feed on the good pasture? Must you also trample the rest of the pasture with your feet?” They shove with flank and shoulder and butt the weak with their horns until the weak are scattered abroad. So God judges “between one sheep and another, between the rams and the goats,” between fat sheep and lean, and promises the lean deliverance: “I will save My flock, and they will no longer be prey. I will judge between one sheep and another.” The restoration, in this book, is not a blanket amnesty sprayed over the nation. It is a sorting, in which the strong who fed on the weak are removed and the preyed-upon are gathered. The same God who said the soul who sins will die now says the sheep who bullied will answer.

The chapter ends by staffing the office it dissolved. “I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will feed them. He will feed them and be their shepherd.” David has been dead for four centuries, and the text gives the title anyway, to the king of David's line whom the tender sprig promised and the removed crown awaits: My servant David. The arrangement is stated twice, as a constitution: “I, the LORD, will be their God, and My servant David will be a prince among them. I, the LORD, have spoken.” Under him comes the covenant of peace: wild animals rid from the land, the flock dwelling securely in the wilderness and sleeping in the forest, and “I will make them and the places around My hill a blessing,” with rain in its season, fruit on the trees, the yoke's bars broken, and no more prey for the nations, no more famine, no more scorn. The chapter that began with shepherds eating the flock ends with the flock confessing its Shepherd in the first person plural of possession: “You are My flock, the sheep of My pasture, My people, and I am your God,’ declares the Lord GOD.”

title: Seir Desolate, the Mountains Alive
subtitle: Ezekiel 35-36
description: Mount Seir is sentenced for gloating over an empty land, and the mountains of Israel, in the same breath, are promised branches, fruit, and people.
paragraphs: Before the restoration can be preached, one neighbor has to be dealt with a second time, because Edom did not merely gloat at the fall; Edom moved in on the estate. “Son of man, set your face against Mount Seir and prophesy against it,” Seir being Edom's mountain country, and the charge is the oldest one in the family: “Because you harbored an ancient hatred and delivered the Israelites over to the sword in the time of their disaster at the final stage of their punishment.” Ancient hatred, Esau's grudge carried for a thousand years, cashed out at Judah's execution by handing fugitives to the sword. The sentence is the lex talionis in God's own words: “Since you did not hate bloodshed, it will pursue you.” Bloodshed for bloodshed, pursuit for pursuit, and the land emptied of traffic forever: “I will make you a perpetual desolation, and your cities will not be inhabited. Then you will know that I am the LORD.”

The specific boast God answers is a property claim made while the owners were being deported. Edom said: “These two nations and countries will be ours, and we will possess them,” Judah and Israel both, the whole inheritance, and the oracle appends to their sentence a clause of five words that undoes it entirely: “even though the LORD was there.” The land was never vacant. Its tenant had been evicted by its Owner, who remained in residence, and Edom's surveyors were measuring another God's estate. God also testifies that He kept the minutes of Edom's celebration: “Then you will know that I, the LORD, have heard every contemptuous word you uttered against the mountains of Israel when you said, ‘They are desolate; they are given to us to devour!’” And then, in a line with no patience left in it: “You boasted against Me with your mouth and multiplied your words against Me. I heard it Myself!”

The measure-for-measure ending is nearly festive: “While the whole earth rejoices, I will make you desolate. As you rejoiced when the inheritance of the house of Israel became desolate, so will I do to you. You will become a desolation, O Mount Seir, and so will all of Edom. Then they will know that I am the LORD.” Rejoicing answered with desolation, desolation answered, in the very next oracle, with joy, because chapter 36 turns the prophet's face from Seir to the mountains of Israel, and the mountains are addressed as the mourners they have been since chapter 6, when Ezekiel prophesied against them for their high places. Now the same mountains get the opposite sermon. The enemy has said of them too: “Aha! The ancient heights have become our possession.” The nations have made them desolate, trampled them, taken them up in slander, turned the land into a byword. God's answer is spoken “in My burning zeal,” the jealousy of the book's marriage language now burning for the land instead of against its people.

The promise to the mountains is agricultural and personal at once. “But you, O mountains of Israel, will produce branches and bear fruit for My people Israel, for they will soon come home.” Branches and fruit, after years of ash, grown for a returning population with an arrival time attached: soon. “For behold, I am on your side; I will turn toward you, and you will be tilled and sown. I will multiply the people upon you,” the whole “house of Israel in its entirety.” “The cities will be inhabited and the ruins rebuilt.” The land will be filled with people and animals and made to prosper more than before, and a slander about the land itself is formally retired: the nations used to say the land devoured its own people and robbed the nation of its children, a land that eats its inhabitants. God revokes the reputation: “you will no longer devour men or deprive your nation of its children,” and the taunts of the nations will no longer be heard against it.

Set side by side, the two oracles are one sermon with two addresses. Seir, which rejoiced over the empty land and claimed it, gets perpetual emptiness. The mountains of Israel, which endured reproach and slander in their emptiness, get branches, fruit, tilling, cities, and children, because their people are coming home. The ground itself is treated as a member of the covenant community, capable of disgrace and of blessing, and the geography of the book's ending is being prepared: a land repopulated, a people to be brought back onto it. What remains is the harder problem, the one chapter 18 posed and the shepherds chapter circled: the people themselves, with their hearts of stone. The next oracle, the second half of chapter 36, is the book's answer, and it is addressed not to mountains but to the house of Israel, and it begins by explaining, with unusual frankness, whose sake the whole restoration is for.

title: A New Heart and a New Spirit
subtitle: Ezekiel 36:16-38
description: The greatest promise in the book: not for Israel's sake but for God's name, clean water, a new heart, and His Spirit put within them.
paragraphs: The greatest promise in Ezekiel begins with a review of the evidence, and the review is not flattering: “when the people of Israel lived in their land, they defiled it by their own ways and deeds.” God poured out His wrath for the blood shed on the land and the idols that defiled it, and scattered them among the nations, judged according to their ways. And there, in exile, the defilement took a new form: “And wherever they went among the nations, they profaned My holy name, because it was said of them, ‘These are the people of the LORD, yet they had to leave His land.’” The exiles' mere existence abroad was a slander against God. The nations read the deportation the way Moab read it: their God could not keep them, or would not, or was like all the other gods. Israel's punishment, deserved in every particular, had become God's public relations disaster, and God says plainly that it concerned Him: “But I had concern for My holy name, which the house of Israel had profaned among the nations to which they had gone.”

So the motive of the restoration is declared before the restoration is, twice, so no one can mistake it for a reward: “It is not for your sake that I will act, O house of Israel, but for My holy name, which you profaned among the nations to which you went. I will show the holiness of My great name, which has been profaned among the nations,” “the name you have profaned among them. Then the nations will know that I am the LORD, declares the Lord GOD, when I show My holiness in you before their eyes.” In you. The people who profaned the name by their exile will vindicate it by their restoration, in front of the same audience. Chapter 20's refrain, I acted for the sake of My name, which explained forty years of wilderness mercy, now explains the entire future: God will act so that the nations' conclusion about Him is corrected, and Israel is the demonstration.

Then the action itself, in a sequence of first-person verbs that leaves Israel with nothing to contribute but presence. “For I will take you from among the nations and gather you out of all the countries, and I will bring you back into your own land. I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean. I will cleanse you from all your impurities and all your idols. I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes and to carefully observe My ordinances.” Take, gather, bring, sprinkle, cleanse, give, remove, put. The new heart commanded in chapter 18, fashion for yourselves a new heart, is here performed by God as surgery, and the obedience that Israel never managed is itself included in the gift: My Spirit within you will cause you to walk in My statutes. Then the covenant formula, the book's destination sentence: “Then you will live in the land that I gave your forefathers; you will be My people, and I will be your God.”

And the people's part, when it finally comes, is not achievement but memory. “Then you will remember your evil ways and wicked deeds, and you will loathe yourselves for your iniquities and abominations.” Grace in Ezekiel does not produce amnesia; it produces the clear-eyed self-disgust that chapter 6 promised from the first remnant, now promised to the whole restored nation. And lest the memory be mistaken for the motive, God drives the nail a second time: “It is not for your sake that I will act, declares the Lord GOD,” let it be known to you: “Be ashamed and disgraced for your ways, O house of Israel!” Shame is not the price of the restoration. It is part of its fruit, the honest atmosphere of a people who know exactly why they are home and exactly why they left.

The results are visible from the road. On the day God cleanses them, the cities are resettled and the ruins rebuilt; the desolate land is cultivated “instead of lying desolate in the sight of all who pass through,” until travelers say the sentence that reverses the whole book: “This land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden. The cities that were once ruined, desolate, and destroyed are now fortified and inhabited.” The nations around will know that the LORD rebuilt what was destroyed and replanted what was desolate: “I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will do it.” And the closing image multiplies the people past agriculture into sheer abundance: God will multiply them like a flock, “so the ruined cities will be filled with flocks of people. Then they will know that I am the LORD.” Flocks of people, grazing in rebuilt cities, under a God who gave them new hearts for His name's sake. The next vision asks the obvious question of a prophet standing among exiles who feel exactly like a graveyard: can a people this dead actually live?

title: Can These Bones Live?
subtitle: Ezekiel 37:1-14
description: A valley of very dry bones, two sermons preached to bones and breath, and a promise the text itself interprets: these bones are the whole house of Israel.
paragraphs: The hand of the LORD takes Ezekiel out by the Spirit and sets him down in the middle of a valley, “and it was full of bones.” The setting is made worse by a guided tour: God leads him “all around among them,” back and forth across the valley floor, so that the prophet registers the two facts the vision is built on: the bones are a great many, and “they were very dry.” Not recently dead, not decaying. Dry. Whatever happened here finished long ago, and nothing about a valley of sun-bleached bones suggests a future. Then God asks the question the whole vision hangs on: “Son of man, can these bones come to life?” And Ezekiel gives the most careful answer in the book: “O Lord GOD,” he replied, “only You know.” It is not faith and it is not unbelief. It is a prophet declining to set the limits of what God can do, in either direction, in a place where all the evidence runs one way.

God's answer to the question is a task. “Prophesy concerning these bones and tell them, ‘Dry bones, hear the word of the LORD!” The audience of the sermon is the bones themselves. And the promise is made in stages, announced in advance: “I will cause breath to enter you, and you will come to life. I will attach tendons to you and make flesh grow upon you and cover you with skin. I will put breath within you so that you will come to life. Then you will know that I am the LORD.” Ezekiel prophesies as commanded, and the valley responds with sound before it responds with life: “there was suddenly a noise, a rattling, and the bones came together, bone to bone.” He watches the assembly complete itself: “tendons appeared on them, flesh grew, and skin covered them; but there was no breath in them.” A valley of perfect corpses. The structure of a nation, rebuilt and recognizable, and dead, because structure is not breath.

So the prophet is sent to preach a second sermon, this one to the breath itself. “Prophesy to the breath; prophesy, son of man, and tell the breath that this is what the Lord GOD says: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe into these slain, so that they may live!” The Hebrew word he is playing on, though the translation keeps it simple, is one word for breath, wind, and spirit, and the vision works in all three registers at once. Ezekiel prophesies, “and the breath entered them, and they came to life and stood on their feet,” a vast army. Two sermons, two stages: the word to the bones makes a body, the word to the breath makes an army. Nothing in the valley came from the bones. Every verb of making belongs to God, and the prophet's only contribution was speech at God's command, addressed to things that could not hear him, which is a summary of his whole ministry to this point.

Then God interprets His own vision, and the interpretation is specific, because the valley is not, in the first instance, about death in general: “Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. Look, they are saying, ‘Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are cut off.’” The exiles' despair from chapter 33 is the dryness. God's counter-sermon to them runs through the grave: “O My people, I will open your graves and bring you up from them, and I will bring you back to the land of Israel. Then you, My people, will know that I am the LORD, when I open your graves and bring you up from them.” And the second stage of the vision is given its name: “I will put My Spirit in you and you will live, and I will settle you in your own land. Then you will know that I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will do it, declares the LORD.”

The book is careful about the picture's limits, and a faithful reading keeps them: the text's own interpretation of the bones is national, a dead people revived and replanted, gathered first and given God's Spirit second, in exactly the order of chapter 36. Later generations would hear more in it, and the images of opened graves and entering breath would feed Israel's and the church's hope of a resurrection of the dead; the vision does not stop them, but the prophet was shown a valley of his own people's bones and told it was the whole house of Israel saying its hope had perished. The God who answered his caution, only You know, has now answered it for the record: the bones can live, because breath is His to give. What remains is to make the revived army one people, and the next sign does it with two sticks and a pen.

title: One Stick in His Hand
subtitle: Ezekiel 37:15-28
description: Two sticks become one in the prophet's hand, one nation under one king, with God's sanctuary in their midst and His covenant of peace forever.
paragraphs: The last sign act of the book is performed with a pen. Ezekiel is told to take a single stick and write on it: “Belonging to Judah and to the Israelites associated with him.” Then a second stick: “Belonging to Joseph,” “the stick of Ephraim,” “and to all the house of Israel associated with him.” Then, “join them together into one stick, so that they become one in your hand.” Writing on wood, the two halves of a nation split since the days after Solomon, Judah in the south and Ephraim, Joseph's tribe standing for the north, carried in one fist as a single piece. The audience of exiles does what audiences of signs are meant to do: “When your people ask you, ‘Won’t you explain to us what you mean by these?’” For once the sign is asked about before the event instead of after, a small sign in itself that the exiles are finally listening like students instead of concertgoers.

The explanation is God's, and it begins with His own hand doing what the prophet's hand pictured: “I will take the stick of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel associated with him, and I will put them together with the stick of Judah. I will make them into a single stick, and they will become one in My hand.” The union is not negotiated between the kingdoms, not a treaty or a merger of the survivors' choosing; the two sticks become one in God's hand, which is the only place they were ever both held. Then the gathering that carries it: “I will take the Israelites out of the nations to which they have gone, and I will gather them from all around and bring them into their own land. I will make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel, and one king will rule over all of them. Then they will no longer be two nations and will never again be divided into two kingdoms.” Three centuries of division, from Jeroboam's calves to Samaria's ashes, are answered with the word never. The split that defined Israel's whole political history is itself declared temporary.

And the union has a holiness condition built into it, or rather built out of it: “They will no longer defile themselves with their idols or detestable images, or with any of their transgressions. I will save them from all their apostasies by which they sinned, and I will cleanse them. Then they will be My people, and I will be their God.” The reunification fails, in every human attempt in the book's background, on exactly this point; men can join sticks, but they cannot cleanse peoples. God does both. The covenant formula closes the verse, the destination of the entire restoration movement: they will be My people, and I will be their God.

The staff of the united nation is the figure who has now been promised three ways: the tender sprig planted by God, the one shepherd of chapter 34, and here the king of the joined sticks: “My servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd for all of them. They will follow My ordinances and keep and observe My statutes.” The tenure is permanent and generational: the people “will live there forever with their children and grandchildren, and My servant David will be their prince forever.” In the land given to Jacob, where their fathers lived, the line of the promise runs unbroken into grandchildren, and the prince's term has no end date. The divided kingdoms had produced nineteen kings in the north, all of them bad, and twenty in the south, most of them failures. The answer is not a better election. It is one King, God's servant, forever.

The oracle, and with it the vision sequence of the valley and the sticks, ends on the thing the glory left behind in chapter 11: “And I will make a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting covenant. I will establish them and multiply them, and I will set My sanctuary among them forever. My dwelling place will be with them; I will be their God, and they will be My people.” The sanctuary among them forever: the presence that departed by stages, threshold, gate, mountain, is promised back as a permanent resident. And the audience of the promise is, one last time, the nations: “Then the nations will know that I the LORD sanctify Israel, when My sanctuary is among them forever.” The exiles' profanation of God's name abroad will be answered by God's sanctification of Israel at home, in public, permanently. One threat remains on the book's horizon before the sanctuary can be shown: an enemy out of the far north, in the latter days, against this very restored and dwelling-securely people. The book deals with him next, before it opens the temple doors.

title: Gog from the Far North
subtitle: Ezekiel 38
description: Out of the far north comes Gog against a restored, unwalled land, and the invasion exists, God says, so that the nations may know Him.
paragraphs: The restored land has one more enemy in the book, and he is the strangest figure in it. “Son of man, set your face against Gog of the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. Prophesy against him and declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I am against you, O Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal.” Meshech and Tubal were peoples of the far north known from the trade lists; their chief prince bears a name, Gog, and a land, Magog, that the text locates at the edge of the map and explains no further. His coalition is assembled from the rim of the known world: Persia, Cush, and Put from the south and east, Gomer and Beth-togarmah “from the far north,” many nations gathered around one leader. And the leash is in God's hand from the first oracle: “I will turn you around, put hooks in your jaws, and bring you out with all your army.” Hooks in the jaws, the same tackle God used on Pharaoh the monster. Gog does not wander south on his own initiative. He is hauled.

The timing is the first thing the oracle insists on, because it places the invasion after the restoration, not during the exile: “After a long time you will be summoned. In the latter years you will enter a land that has recovered from war, whose people were gathered from many nations to the mountains of Israel, which had long been desolate. They had been brought out from the nations, and all now dwell securely.” The land of chapters 36 and 37, repopulated, rebuilt, at peace, is the target. Against it the horde advances “like a thunderstorm,” “like a cloud covering the land,” the weather metaphors of judgment turned now against God's enemies. The invasion belongs to the latter days of the book's own timeline of restoration, a final assault on the finished work, which is why the book places it here, after the covenant of peace and before the temple: the last enemy is met before the last vision opens.

Gog's motive is given in his own planning, and it is pure plunder. “On that day, thoughts will arise in your mind, and you will devise an evil plan.” The plan, in his own words: “I will go up against a land of unwalled villages; I will come against a quiet people who dwell securely, all of them living without walls or bars or gates,” coming “in order to seize the spoil and carry off the plunder.” The restored people's security is the opportunity: unwalled villages, livestock and possessions acquired, a people living “at the center of the land.” Even the trading nations smell the motive and ask it aloud: “Sheba and Dedan and the merchants of Tarshish with all its villages will ask, ‘Have you come to capture the plunder?” Tyre's old partners, reduced to asking questions from the sidelines. Gog comes for loot, against a people whose defenses the book has deliberately described as God Himself, their shepherd, their sanctuary, their prince. The mismatch is the point.

And God's motive is stated as plainly as Gog's, in the oracle's purpose clause: “It will happen in the latter days, O Gog, that I will bring you against My land, so that the nations may know Me when I show Myself holy in you before their eyes.” In you: Gog's destruction will be the display case of God's holiness, the final and largest instance of the book's refrain. God even taunts him with antiquity: “Are you the one of whom I have spoken in former days through My servants, the prophets of Israel, who in those times prophesied for years that I would bring you against them?” The text does not name those prophecies, and Gog stands in the book as its own witness: identified by God, located by the text at the far north in the latter days, and left there. Every later attempt to pin modern nations and leaders onto his coalition is interpretation laid over the text, and the text itself keeps its own counsel about his address and era beyond what it says.

The battle, when it comes, is fought by God in the elements. “My wrath will flare up. In My zeal and fiery rage I proclaim that on that day there will be a great earthquake in the land of Israel,” so that fish and birds and beasts and every crawling thing and all mankind tremble at His presence: “The mountains will be thrown down, the cliffs will collapse, and every wall will fall to the ground.” Then confusion does the ground fighting: “every man’s sword will be against his brother,” the coalition turning on itself on God's mountains, and heaven finishes the work: “I will execute judgment upon him with plague and bloodshed. I will pour out torrents of rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur on him and on his troops and on the many nations with him.” The restored people never lift a weapon in the chapter. Their shepherd fights it entire. And the last verse is the refrain raised to its highest pitch in the book: “I will magnify and sanctify Myself, and I will reveal Myself in the sight of many nations. Then they will know that I am the LORD.” The next chapter counts the cost of the cleanup, and it takes seven years.

title: Seven Years, Seven Months
subtitle: Ezekiel 39
description: Seven years of burning weapons and seven months of burial clear Gog's battlefield, and the book's restoration ends with God's face hidden no longer.
