paragraphs: Chapter 39 is the sequel told in logistics, and it opens with the disarming. “Then I will strike the bow from your left hand and dash down the arrows from your right hand.” Gog falls on the mountains of Israel with all his troops and the nations with him, given as food to every kind of ravenous bird and wild beast, fallen in the open field “for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.” And the judgment travels home with the news: “I will send fire on Magog and on those who dwell securely in the coastlands, and they will know that I am the LORD.” Then the motive that has governed the restoration movement is stated over the battlefield: “So I will make My holy name known among My people Israel and will no longer allow it to be profaned. Then the nations will know that I am the LORD, the Holy One in Israel.” The name profaned by the exile, defended by the gathering, is now defended by the destruction of the last invader, and the title God takes in the sentence is the book's summary of Him: the Holy One in Israel.

The cleanup is where the oracle gets its title numbers. Israel's cities will go out and burn the captured weapons for fuel: “the bucklers and shields, the bows and arrows, the clubs and spears. For seven years they will use them for fuel.” Seven years without gathering wood from the countryside or cutting from the forests, a whole economy heated by the wreckage of the invasion: “They will loot those who looted them and plunder those who plundered them, declares the Lord GOD.” The burial takes seven months of the whole nation's labor, “in order to cleanse the land,” in a valley east of the Sea renamed for the multitude buried in it, the Valley of Hamon-gog, with a city nearby called Hamonah. Professional searchers will be employed after the seven months to pass through the land, and anyone who finds a human bone “will set up a pillar next to it, until the gravediggers have buried it.” The land's cleansing is a public works project, and God attaches honor to it: it will bring the people renown “on the day I display My glory.”

The strangest scene follows, a banquet God hosts. He calls every bird and beast to a sacrificial feast on the mountains of Israel: “Assemble and come together from all around to the sacrificial feast that I am preparing for you, a great feast on the mountains of Israel. There you will eat flesh and drink blood. You will eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the princes of the earth.” They will eat fat until gorged and drink blood until drunk, horses and riders, mighty men and warriors of every kind, at God's table. The imagery is deliberately shocking, a sacrifice in reverse, where the invading army is the offering and the carrion creatures are the guests, and it completes the arc that began when God gave Pharaoh's carcass to the beasts and birds in the desert. What God begins against the proud, He finishes at His own table, on His own mountains.

Then the oracle states the lesson in both directions, because two audiences have been misreading the exile for a generation. For Israel: “From that day forward the house of Israel will know that I am the LORD their God.” For the nations, the explanation they got wrong in chapter 36 is corrected on the record: “And the nations will know that the house of Israel went into exile for their iniquity, because they were unfaithful to Me. So I hid My face from them and delivered them into the hands of their enemies, so that they all fell by the sword. I dealt with them according to their uncleanness and transgressions, and I hid My face from them.” The exile was not God's weakness. It was God's judgment, and the nations will know it from the scale of the restoration that reverses it. Both misreadings, Israel's despair and the nations' contempt, are answered in one battle and one burial.

The chapter, and the restoration movement with it, ends with the book's fullest statement of the return. “Now I will restore Jacob from captivity and will have compassion on the whole house of Israel, and I will be jealous for My holy name.” The restored will forget their disgrace in security, with no one to frighten them, and God will show His holiness in them “in the sight of many nations” as He gathers them out of the lands of their enemies, “not leaving any of them behind after their exile among the nations.” Not one left behind; the gathering of chapter 36 is here made exhaustive. And the final verse answers the glory's departure across thirty chapters: “And I will no longer hide My face from them, for I will pour out My Spirit on the house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD.” Face hidden in judgment, face restored in mercy, and the Spirit, promised to the dry bones and the new heart, poured out on the whole house. The book has one vision left, the longest and most detailed of all, and it begins with a man of bronze holding a measuring rod, in a city whose temple God has come home to.

title: The Man of Bronze
subtitle: Ezekiel 40-42
description: In the twenty-fifth year of exile a man of bronze with a measuring reed walks Ezekiel through walls, gates, and courts, and the tour keeps climbing.
paragraphs: The book's last vision is dated with double precision, as if God wanted the timing weighed: “In the twenty-fifth year of our exile, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month,” in “the fourteenth year after Jerusalem had been struck down,” “on that very day the hand of the LORD was upon me.” Twenty-five years into exile, fourteen years after the fall, halfway through a captivity Jeremiah had numbered at seventy. The exiles are settled, aging, some born in Babylon. Ezekiel is carried in visions of God to the land of Israel and set on a very high mountain, and on its southern slope is a structure like a city. A man is standing in its gateway waiting for him: “I saw a man whose appearance was like bronze. He was standing in the gateway with a linen cord and a measuring rod in his hand.” Bronze like the gleam of the living creatures' feet in chapter 1, a figure from the glory's own world, holding the tools of a surveyor. His charge to the prophet defines the whole vision: “look with your eyes, hear with your ears, and pay attention to everything I am going to show you, for that is why you have been brought here. Report to the house of Israel everything you see.” Ezekiel's last assignment is to be a measuring witness. What follows, for nine chapters, is measurement.

The tour starts with a wall and a gate, and the gate gets more verses than the temple building itself. The wall around the temple area is one rod thick and one rod high, the rod being six long cubits, a cubit and a handbreadth each. The east gate is climbed by steps and measured room by room: threshold one rod deep, three gate chambers on each side, each one rod square, windows beveled in the walls, side pillars decorated with palm trees, a portico facing the temple, fifty cubits from entrance to inner end. Then the outer court: chambers and a pavement all around, thirty chambers facing the pavement, and a hundred cubits from the lower gateway to the inner court. The north gate and the south gate are measured next, and the refrain of the chapters begins to beat: the same measurements as the others. Order is the vision's first doctrine. Whatever this place is, it is not improvised; it has been drawn, completely, before it is described, and the prophet's job is to take down the drawing faithfully.

The inner gates have eight steps where the outer gates have seven, and the tour keeps climbing toward holiness by numbers. Inside the inner gateways are chambers where the burnt offering is washed, and tables, four inside and four outside each gateway, “on which the sacrifices were to be slaughtered,” plus four tables of dressed stone for the burnt offering with the slaughtering utensils laid on them and double-pronged hooks fastened around the room “and the flesh of the offering was to be placed on the tables.” This temple is no monument and no metaphor-machine; it is a working house of sacrifice, designed down to the hooks meat hangs on. By the inner court stand two chambers assigned already to their staff: the south-facing for the priests who keep charge of the temple, the north-facing for the priests who keep charge of the altar, “These are the sons of Zadok, the only Levites who may approach the LORD to minister before Him.” The inner court measures a hundred cubits square, the altar stands before the temple, and the portico is reached by ten steps, the climb still rising.

Chapter 41 measures the house itself. The outer sanctuary is forty cubits long and twenty wide, the same footprint as Solomon's holy place, and the man goes in alone to measure the room beyond and announces it in the vision's most solemn sentence: “This is the Most Holy Place,” twenty cubits square. The temple wall is six cubits thick. Around it run side rooms in three levels of thirty, widening as they rise, resting on ledges built into the wall's thickness “so that the supports would not be fastened into the wall of the temple itself,” the holy building not even pierced by its own annexes. The interior is paneled in wood and carved from floor to windows with cherubim and palm trees in alternation, and the cherubim of this temple have a new anatomy: “Each cherub had two faces: the face of a man was toward the palm tree on one side, and the face of a young lion was toward the palm tree on the other side.” Man and lion, two of the four faces from the River Kebar, carved now in stillness on the walls of the house the glory left. Before the inner sanctuary stands a wooden altar, three cubits high, and the guide names it with a sentence that reaches back to the tabernacle: “This is the table that is before the LORD.”

Chapter 42 finishes the buildings with the priests' chambers on the north and south, three stories of galleries facing the temple courtyard. “The north and south chambers facing the temple courtyard are the holy chambers where the priests who approach the LORD will eat the most holy offerings,” and the holiness is handled with a care the old temple had lost: “Once the priests have entered the holy area, they must not go out into the outer court until they have left behind the garments in which they minister, for these are holy. They are to put on other clothes before they approach the places that are for the people.” Holiness in this vision is almost physical, a charge carried on cloth, not to be tracked casually into common ground. Then the man measures the whole enclosure: five hundred cubits on each side, a perfect square, walled, and the last verse of the tour states what all the cubits were for: “It had a wall all around, five hundred cubits long and five hundred cubits wide, to separate the holy from the common.” In the old city, priests made no distinction between the holy and the common, and the whole land became common and then desolate. The new house is drawn as one long distinction, five hundred cubits square. And as the prophet stands in the measured courts, the east gate he entered by is about to be used by Someone else.

title: The Glory Returns
subtitle: Ezekiel 43
description: The sound of rushing waters returns from the east: the glory enters by the gate it left, and the throne declares it will never depart again.
paragraphs: The man brings Ezekiel back to the gate facing east, the gate of the glory's departure, and the book's longest arc closes in one verse: “and I saw the glory of the God of Israel coming from the east. His voice was like the roar of many waters, and the earth shone with His glory.” From the east, the direction of the Mount of Olives where the glory had stood looking back at the city it left. The sound is the sound of chapter 1, the wings like many waters, now identified as His voice. And Ezekiel himself supplies the book's own cross-references, the only time he annotates his visions this way: “The vision I saw was like the vision I had seen when He came to destroy the city and like the visions I had seen by the River Kebar. I fell facedown.” Like the Kebar vision, and like the destroy-the-city vision, the temple tour of chapters 8 to 11 read backwards: the same glory that arrived in exile to announce judgment and departed the temple in stages has come back along its own route, and the prophet falls facedown for the third time before it.

The entry is precise about the door: “and the glory of the LORD entered the temple through the gate facing east,” the east gate, the very gate it paused at on the way out, and “Then the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple.” Filled: the word the old histories used for the tabernacle and for Solomon's temple, the cloud of presence taking up residence. Then, while the bronze man stands beside him, Ezekiel hears Someone speaking from inside the temple, the voice now located in the house: “Son of man, this is the place of My throne and the place for the soles of My feet, where I will dwell among the Israelites forever.” The traveling throne of chapter 1, the chariot that could go anywhere without turning, announces its parking place: here, forever.

And the permanence is paired with the past in one breath: “The house of Israel will never again defile My holy name,” “neither they nor their kings,” “by their prostitution and by the funeral offerings for their kings at their deaths,” the kings who had buried their dead beside the sanctuary and set “their threshold next to My threshold and their doorposts beside My doorposts, with only a wall between Me and them.” The old intimacy was defilement, the palace hard against the temple wall. The new order starts with distance and cleansing: “Now let them remove far from Me their prostitution and the funeral offerings for their kings, and I will dwell among them forever.”

Then God explains what the nine-chapter measuring exercise was for, and the answer is not architecture. “As for you, son of man, describe the temple to the people of Israel, so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities. Let them measure the plan.” The blueprint is a sermon: the exiles are to study the design of a house they have never seen and be ashamed, the measured holiness of the place confronting the measured account of their sins. “and if they are ashamed of all they have done, then make known to them the design of the temple,” “its arrangement and its exits and entrances,” “its whole design along with all its statutes, forms, and laws. Write it down in their sight, so that they may keep its complete design and all its statutes and may carry them out.” Shame first, then the full plan, then obedience: the vision's own order of operations, the same order as chapter 36, where memory and loathing followed the gift. And over the whole complex God pronounces its constitution: “This is the law of the temple: All its surrounding territory on top of the mountain will be most holy. Yes, this is the law of the temple.” Not a holy building on common ground. The entire mountaintop, most holy, ground and house together.

The chapter ends at the altar, measured in its tiers: a base and gutter, a lower ledge two cubits up, a larger ledge four cubits more, a hearth four cubits high and twelve cubits square with four horns projecting upward, its steps facing east, toward the gate the glory entered. Then the consecration statute, the temple's first week of operation: “You are to give a young bull from the herd as a sin offering to the Levitical priests who are of the family of Zadok, who approach Me to minister before Me,” its blood put on the horns and corners and rim “thus you will cleanse the altar and make atonement for it.” A goat the second day, and for seven days the priests make atonement for the altar and consecrate it with daily offerings. “At the end of these days, from the eighth day on, the priests are to present your burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar. Then I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD.” Then I will accept you. After forty-three chapters, the sentence the whole book has been traveling toward is spoken from inside the filled temple, and the visions that remain are its working out: who may serve in such a house, how its land is shared, and what flows out of it into the world.

title: The Shut Gate and the Sons of Zadok
subtitle: Ezekiel 44
description: The east gate stays shut because God has entered through it, failed priests are demoted, and the sons of Zadok receive a stricter, linen code.
paragraphs: The chapter opens at the gate the glory used, and it is closed. “The man then brought me back to the outer gate of the sanctuary that faced east, but it was shut. And the LORD said to me, ‘This gate is to remain shut. It shall not be opened, and no man shall enter through it, because the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered through it. Therefore it will remain shut.” A door sealed forever by the memory of Who came through it: the east gate becomes a monument, untrafficable, because God's entrance has made it holy the way the burning bush made ground holy. One exception is named, and it is carefully fenced: “Only the prince himself may sit inside the gateway to eat in the presence of the LORD. He must enter by way of the portico of the gateway and go out the same way.” The prince eats there; he does not pass through. Even royalty sits down in the doorway rather than using God's door as a corridor. Ezekiel is then taken by the north gate to the front of the temple, and “I looked and saw the glory of the LORD filling His temple, and I fell facedown,” a fourth time, and from the ground he receives the personnel code of the new house.

It begins with an audit of the old one. “I have had enough of all your abominations, O house of Israel.” The particular charge named is outsourcing: Israel “brought in foreigners uncircumcised in both heart and flesh to occupy My sanctuary,” defiling the temple at the moment of offering, and worse, “you have not kept charge of My holy things, but have appointed others to keep charge of My sanctuary for you.” The keepers delegated the keeping. The new rule is flat: “No foreigner uncircumcised in heart and flesh may enter My sanctuary,” “not even a foreigner who lives among the Israelites.” And inside the people, the sorting runs by history. The Levites who “wandered away from Me when Israel went astray, and who wandered away from Me after their idols, will bear the consequences of their iniquity.” They are not expelled; they are demoted with precision: “Yet they shall be ministers in My sanctuary, having charge of the gates of the temple and ministering there. They shall slaughter the burnt offerings and other sacrifices for the people and stand before them to minister to them.” Gates and slaughter, service to the people, real work, but: “They must not approach Me to serve Me as priests or come near any of My holy things or the most holy things. They will bear the shame of the abominations they have committed.” In the new house, your past is your posting.

Over against them stand the men who stayed. “But the Levitical priests, who are descended from Zadok and who kept charge of My sanctuary when the Israelites went astray from Me, are to approach Me to minister before Me. They will stand before Me to offer Me fat and blood, declares the Lord GOD. They alone shall enter My sanctuary and draw near to My table to minister before Me. They will keep My charge.” Zadok's line had kept the altar through the apostasy, and the reward is nearness itself.

Their working code is then given in detail, and every line of it is a distinction: linen garments in the inner court, no wool, nothing “that makes them perspire”; linen turbans; the ministering garments left in the holy chambers and changed before going out to the people, “so that they do not transmit holiness to the people with their garments”; hair neither shaved nor grown long but carefully trimmed; no wine before entering; marriage restricted to virgins of Israel or priests' widows. And their teaching office is named as the reversal of the old priesthood's failure: “They are to teach My people the difference between the holy and the common and show them how to discern between the clean and the unclean,” the exact distinction chapter 22 said the priests had collapsed. They will judge disputes by God's ordinances, keep the feasts and Sabbaths, and observe strict rules about contact with the dead.

Their pay is the chapter's last word, and it is not land. “In regard to their inheritance, I am their inheritance. You are to give them no possession in Israel, for I am their possession.” The priests of the new house own nothing in the land the next chapters will divide so carefully; their portion is God Himself, supplemented by the offerings and the firstfruits, “The best of all the firstfruits,” and the first batch of every household's dough, “so that a blessing may rest upon your homes.” Landless by design, attached to the sanctuary the way the sanctuary is attached to the mountain, the sons of Zadok close the personnel code where the vision's geography began: with holiness assigned an address and a staff who kept charge when keeping it cost something. The remaining chapters widen from the staff to the whole country: the land grant around the temple, the prince's rules, the feasts, and then the river.

title: Enough, O Princes
subtitle: Ezekiel 45-46
description: The country is drawn around the sanctuary, the princes are told enough, and the last laws keep the throne from ever taking a small man's inheritance.
paragraphs: Chapters 45 and 46 draw the country around the sanctuary, and the drawing is a political constitution. When the land is divided by lot, a holy portion is set aside first, before any tribe is named: “you are to set aside a portion for the LORD, a holy portion of the land 25,000 cubits long and 20,000 cubits wide. This entire tract of land will be holy.” Inside it, nested like the courts themselves, lie the sanctuary on its five-hundred-cubit square, a strip twenty-five thousand by ten thousand for the priests who draw near, with their houses, an adjacent strip of the same size for the Levites and their towns, and a strip five thousand wide for the city, belonging “to the whole house of Israel.” And flanking the whole sacred district on both sides, running to the eastern and western borders of the country, is the prince's land. His possession is generous and it is fenced by the sanctuary itself: on both sides of him, before he reaches any tribe, stands God's portion. The geography preaches before a single law is given. Power in this country lives next door to holiness, and holiness is not negotiable ground.

Then God addresses the office directly, and the address is a rebuke aimed backward across the whole book: “Enough, O princes of Israel! Cease your violence and oppression, and do what is just and right. Stop dispossessing My people, declares the Lord GOD.” Enough: the audit word for four centuries of kings. And the land grant that precedes it carries the promise the audit was working toward: “And My princes will no longer oppress My people, but will give the rest of the land to the house of Israel according to their tribes.” The first royal legislation of the new order is not about palaces or armies. It is about weights: “You must use honest scales, a just ephah, and a just bath.” The ephah and bath fixed at a tenth of a homer, the shekel at twenty gerahs, the mina defined. In a book where princes devoured people and officials destroyed lives for dishonest gain, the restored kingdom's founding statute standardizes the measuring cups. Justice in Ezekiel's future is not a sentiment. It is metrology.

The prince's job description follows, and it is liturgical and financial rather than military. The people bring a contribution, a fraction of wheat, barley, oil, and one sheep from each flock of two hundred, and “it shall be the prince’s part to provide the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and drink offerings for the feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths,” “for all the appointed feasts of the house of Israel.” He funds the calendar of worship and provides the sin offerings “to make atonement for the house of Israel,” a royal priesthood of provision, not of sacrifice, since the sacrificing belongs to Zadok's sons. The year opens with the sanctuary itself purified: a bull's blood on the doorposts of the temple, the corners of the altar, the gateposts of the inner court, “on the seventh day of the month for anyone who strays unintentionally or in ignorance. In this way you will make atonement for the temple.” Even unintentional sin has a provision and a date. Passover comes on the fourteenth day with its seven days of unleavened bread and the prince's daily bulls and rams and goats, and the feast of the seventh month receives “the same provision,” the year of worship carried on the prince's budget like a public utility.

Chapter 46 gives the weekly rhythm. The inner court's east gate “must be kept shut during the six days of work, but on the Sabbath day and on the day of the New Moon it shall be opened.” The prince enters from outside through the portico, stands by the gatepost while the priests offer his sacrifices, and “He is to bow in worship at the threshold of the gate and then depart, but the gate must not be shut until evening.” The people worship at the same entrance on Sabbaths and New Moons, and the traffic of worship is made one-way: “whoever enters by the north gate to worship must go out by the south gate, and whoever enters by the south gate must go out by the north gate. No one is to return through the gate by which he entered, but each must go out by the opposite gate.” No backtracking in the house of God; you leave by a different door than you came. The prince goes in and out with the people, in their midst, not above them. And every morning, without feast or occasion, a year-old lamb is offered with its grain and oil: “This is a permanent statute,” the daily heartbeat under the calendar.

The chapter's last laws protect the small landowner from the throne, in terms that answer the monarchy's oldest scandal. “The prince must not take any of the inheritance of the people by evicting them from their property. He is to provide an inheritance for his sons from his own property, so that none of My people will be displaced from his property.” No more Naboth's vineyard. What the prince gives his sons stays theirs; what he gives a servant reverts in the year of freedom; the people's portions are beyond his reach entirely. Then the tour ends, almost domestically, in kitchens: a place at the north chambers “where the priests shall boil the guilt offering and the sin offering, and where they shall bake the grain offering, so that they do not bring them into the outer court and transmit holiness to the people,” and in the outer court's four corners, four enclosed kitchen courts with ovens around their walls: “These are the kitchens where those who minister at the temple will cook the sacrifices offered by the people.” The most detailed building code in the Bible finishes in the cooking rooms, because the house it describes is meant to be lived in, fed in, and used. What remains is the land itself, and the water that will run through it.

title: The River
subtitle: Ezekiel 47:1-12
description: Water trickles from the temple threshold, deepens past measuring, and heals the Dead Sea, while the swamps are honestly left to salt.
paragraphs: The tour's last wonder begins as almost nothing. The man brings Ezekiel back to the entrance of the temple, “and I saw water flowing from under the threshold of the temple toward the east.” Not a fountain, not a flood: water coming down “from under the south side of the temple, south of the altar,” slipping out under the threshold of the filled house. Ezekiel is taken out through the north gate and led around the outside wall to the outer east gate, and there the water is “trickling out from the south side.” A trickle. The guide unrolls his measuring line, the same instrument that has measured every wall and gate of the vision, and walks east, and the measuring of the river becomes the vision's final sermon, delivered in depths.

A thousand cubits out, he leads Ezekiel through “ankle-deep water.” Another thousand: knee-deep. Another thousand: waist-deep. “Once again he measured off a thousand cubits, but now it was a river that I could not cross, because the water had risen and was deep enough for swimming.” A river that cannot be crossed on foot, grown out of a trickle, in three thousand cubits of desert, with no tributary, no spring, no rainfall named anywhere along its course. The water deepens by itself, because of where it comes from. The guide's question is the tour's last exam: “Son of man, do you see this?” Then he leads the prophet back along the bank, and the banks have changed since the walk out: “When I arrived, I saw a great number of trees along both banks of the river.” The river makes its own landscape as it goes.

The guide explains the destination. “This water flows out to the eastern region and goes down into the Arabah. When it empties into the Dead Sea, the water there becomes fresh.” The Arabah is the rift valley running down to the Dead Sea, the lowest body of water on earth, so salt-dense that nothing lives in it, the sea of the plain where Sodom stood. Into that dead water the temple's river flows, and the text states the result in the flat tone of a measurement: the water there becomes fresh. “Wherever the river flows, there will be swarms of living creatures and a great number of fish, because it flows there and makes the waters fresh; so wherever the river flows, everything will flourish.” The deadest place in the geography of the Bible becomes a fishery: “Fishermen will stand by the shore; from En-gedi to En-eglaim they will spread their nets to catch fish of many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea.” En-gedi, the oasis halfway down the western shore, to En-eglaim at the north: nets spread again, the same verb the Tyre oracle used for the bare rock, now returned to its proper business, catching fish in water that used to kill everything.

The vision keeps one honest exception, because Ezekiel's promises never airbrush: “But the swamps and marshes will not become fresh; they will be left for salt.” Salt has its place in this world, for covenant and for cooking, and the marshes keep it. Not every corner is transformed in the same way, and the text says so in the middle of its most miraculous paragraph, a prophet's footnote that keeps the wonder credible. Then the trees again, now described in full: “Along both banks of the river, fruit trees of all kinds will grow. Their leaves will not wither, and their fruit will not fail. Each month they will bear fruit, because the water from the sanctuary flows to them. Their fruit will be used for food and their leaves for healing.” Fruit monthly, out of season and in, leaves medicinal, and the reason given is hydrological and theological in one clause: because the water from the sanctuary flows to them.

The river is the temple vision's answer to the book's first vision. By the River Kebar, in exile, God showed Ezekiel a glory that could travel, wheels and wings and eyes, because His people were in a place where no water of life ran. Here, at the end, the glory has come home and sat down, and the house it fills overflows: holiness that has been measured, walled, gated, and guarded for nine chapters turns out, at the threshold, to be leaking life into the desert, deepening as it goes, until the Dead Sea lives. The remaining verses divide the land the river waters, and end the book with an address: a city, and the name over its gates.

title: The LORD Is There
subtitle: Ezekiel 47:13-48:35
description: The land is divided band by band, foreigners inherit beside native-born sons, and the last measurement of the book becomes a name: the LORD Is There.
paragraphs: The book ends with a land survey. “These are the boundaries by which you are to divide the land as an inheritance among the twelve tribes of Israel; Joseph shall receive two portions.” The borders are drawn by compass point: the north from the Great Sea by way of Hethlon through Lebo-hamath to Zedad, the east along the Jordan between Gilead and the land of Israel down to Tamar, the south from Tamar to the waters of Meribath-kadesh and along the Brook of Egypt to the Great Sea, the west the Great Sea itself. The twelve tribes are back in the frame, all of them, the northern kingdom that fell a century and a half before Ezekiel prophesied counted in the inheritance as if Assyria were a parenthesis. “You are to divide it equally among them. Because I swore with an uplifted hand to give it to your forefathers, this land will fall to you as an inheritance.” Equally: the portions of chapter 48 will be parallel bands, tribe by tribe, the same width from the sea to the Jordan, a geometry of fairness no conqueror ever imposed.

Inside the survey sits the most startling clause in the book's constitution, the more startling for its dry legal phrasing: “You shall allot it as an inheritance for yourselves and for the foreigners who dwell among you and who have children. You are to treat them as native-born Israelites; along with you, they shall be allotted an inheritance among the tribes of Israel. In whatever tribe a foreigner dwells, you are to assign his inheritance there,” declares the Lord GOD.” In the old law, the foreigner was protected, fed, and loved, but the land was Israel's by tribe and could not permanently leave the tribe. Here, in the restored land, the resident foreigner who has raised children in a tribe receives a landed inheritance inside that tribe, as native-born. The book that began with a God who would not let Israel dissolve among the nations ends with a nation porous enough to deed its inheritance to the outsiders living within it.

Chapter 48 lays the bands down in order. Seven tribes run across the north in parallel strips: Dan, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, Reuben, and Judah, each “one portion bordering the territory” of the last, “from east to west.” Bordering Judah on the south lies the holy portion, twenty-five thousand cubits wide, with the sanctuary standing in its center, and inside it the priests' strip is singled out with its history attached: “It will be for the consecrated priests, the descendants of Zadok, who kept My charge and did not go astray as the Levites did when the Israelites went astray,” a most holy portion that may never change hands: “They must not sell or exchange any of it, and they must not transfer this best part of the land, for it is holy to the LORD.” The Levites' strip borders it, then the city's common land with the city at its center, then the prince's remainder running to both borders, the sacred district held in the middle of the country like a stone in a setting. South of it, five more bands complete the twelve: Benjamin, Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun, and Gad, down to the southern border at Tamar and the Brook of Egypt. “This is the land you are to allot as an inheritance to the tribes of Israel, and these will be their portions,” declares the Lord GOD.”

The city itself is measured last, and it is the vision's final piece of symmetry: 4,500 cubits on each side, a perfect square, with pastureland extending 250 cubits in every direction, its food grown on the strips east and west by workers drawn “from all the tribes of Israel.” And its gates are its census: “the gates of the city will be named after the tribes of Israel,” three to a side: Reuben, Judah, and Levi on the north; Joseph, Benjamin, and Dan on the east; Simeon, Issachar, and Zebulun on the south; Gad, Asher, and Naphtali on the west. All twelve names over the gates, Levi the priestly tribe and Joseph the double tribe included, no name missing, no tribe's gate bricked up. The nation that split into two kingdoms and scattered into every nation on earth will enter its capital through gates that remember everybody.

Then the last verse of Ezekiel, and the last measurement in the book, and a name: “The perimeter of the city will be 18,000 cubits, and from that day on the name of the city will be: THE LORD IS THERE.” Jerusalem is not even given its old name back. It is renamed for the fact that defines it: the presence that left by the east gate in chapter 11 and returned through it in chapter 43 has become the city's identity, its address, its title deed. Set the book's two ends side by side. It opens by a river in Babylon, among exiles, with the heavens opening over a priest who has no temple: the glory, impossibly, was there, in the wrong country, on wheels. It closes with the glory seated, the river flowing out of its house into the Dead Sea, the land divided in fairness, the foreigner deeded in, and a city whose name is the answer to every “Aha!” the nations ever said over it. The refrain that sounded seventy times, then you will know that I am the LORD, resolves into three words over the gates. The prophet who was told to report everything he saw has reported it. His book closes. The runner of the series now turns to another court prophet of the same exile, a younger man in Babylon itself, whose story begins with a king's dinner and a refusal, and whose God shuts the mouths of lions.
